sentences.text: VisioCrypt: A TEE-Anchored Client-Side Searchable Encryption Scheme with Dynamic V olume-Hiding Padding for Mobile Cloud Storage Anonymous Author(s) Abstract—Most of us back up personal photos and files onto Google Drive or Dropbox without thinking twice.
Yet handing raw data over to cloud companies exposes everything if those servers get breached.
Encrypting everything locally sounds great until someone needs to search for an old receipt.
Downloading the entire database to the phone for every single search burns mobile data and drains the battery.
Instead, the phone sends encrypted search tokens so the cloud finds files blindly.
The catch is that normal search tells the server how many files matched.
A nosy cloud admin can watch these numbers over time to figure out what someone is looking for.
We stop this by padding result lists up to powers of two.
Because every result size looks the same, the server cannot tell common words apart from rare ones.
The server only ever sees bucket sizes of four, eight, sixteen, or thirtytwo items.
We enforce a lower floor of four items on smaller candidate lists.
Deleted files get recorded in a local phone filter without alerting the cloud.
Every new file gets a fresh version number so nobody can link it to older queries.
Random pauses between queries stop eavesdroppers from tracking search timing.
On Android, runtime garbage collection lets discarded keys sit in phone RAM for minutes.
We wipe key arrays in RAM with zeros right after every cipher call.
Our root key stays locked inside ARM TrustZone behind a fingerprint sensor.
Our security proof confirms that search tokens leak nothing to attackers.
We wrote the app in Dart and ran tests on four Android phones.
File encryption hit 310 megabytes per second on the Redmi K80.
Looking up words took 0.23 milliseconds on the K80 and 1.48 milliseconds on the Galaxy A14.
Our in-memory Bloom filter handled over twenty-two thousand membership checks per millisecond.
The extra index entries take up barely a few megabytes on flash storage.
Index Terms—Mobile storage security, encrypted search, dynamic volume hiding, hardware enclaves, memory safety.
INTRODUCTION We store everything from family photos to bank statements on our phones.
Backing up files to Google Drive or Dropbox feels natural and convenient.
If Dropbox or Google servers get hacked, all those personal files leak out in plain text , .
Encrypting files on the phone protects data before it ever hits the internet.
Finding an old receipt inside an encrypted archive is surprisingly painful.
Downloading the whole archive just to run a search on the phone drains mobile data and kills the battery.
Searchable ciphers let the cloud search files without reading our plain text , .
Unfortunately, cloud servers still count how many files match each search.
A rogue admin watching these numbers can quickly guess what words we searched for –.
Sending the same token repeatedly also lets eavesdroppers map out search habits , .
On Android, runtime garbage collection lets discarded keys sit in memory for minutes , .
We built VisioCrypt to keep phone searches safe from cloud snooping.
We pad search results to powers of two so the cloud cannot track match counts.
We track new and deleted files locally so the cloud learns nothing about updates.
We wipe secret keys from RAM with zeros right after every cipher call.
We anchor root keys inside ARM TrustZone behind a fingerprint sensor.
We tested lookups on four real phones, getting sub-millisecond results with barely any battery use.
Song showed how to search encrypted files without decrypting them , , .
Cash made boolean queries fast across large indexes .
Leakage-Abuse Attacks and Volume Mitigation.
Watching search match counts lets attackers reconstruct full databases –, , .
Schemes like SEAL and SW AT tried grouping results into bins to limit volume leakage , , .
Our scheme rounds search lists to powers of two on the phone without needing cloud enclaves .
Forward and Backward Privacy.
Sophos added forward privacy so old queries never find newly added files .
Diana added backward privacy so deleted documents stay hidden from future searches .
Our phone tracks file updates locally using version counters and a Bloom filter.
Hardware-Assisted Security and Mobile Memory Hygiene.
VisioLock locks secret keys to physical phone hardware .
Other researchers tried running searchable encryption inside ARM TrustZone enclaves , , .
Surprisingly, few works investigate how long secret keys linger inside phone RAM after searches finish.

Master Key Derivation The phone derives four separate sub-keys from root secret Kusing HKDF-SHA256: Unique salt labels guarantee that each derived key handles a single cryptographic task.
Power-of-Two Volume-Hiding Padding Policy To stop match count leakage, the phone pads candidate lists to powers of two.
We add dummy entries so every result list has four, eight, sixteen, or thirty-two items.
Rare words stay hidden because list sizes look identical across terms.
This completely hides exact match counts from the remote server.
The cloud server observes only uniform bucket sizes of four, eight, sixteen, or thirty-two items.

•Game 2: Replaces document ciphertextsC i with uniform random noise of identical lengths.

•Game 3: Replaces encrypted multi-map payloads with encrypted zero blocks padded to|Pad(L w)|.

Because|Pad(L w)|produces identical distributions for any two candidate sets within the same power-of-two bin,Game 3 andGame 4 are statistically indistinguishable except for Bloom filter false positives:|Pr[Game 3]−Pr[Game 4]| ≤P e.
